q: Our findings show that Cursor can generate functional large-scale projects
r: Include: controlled empirical evaluation of an agentic AI IDE building project-level applications from requirements, with quality measured by static analysis.

q: We propose ABTest, a behavior-driven fuzzing framework that turns real-world agent failures into reusable, repository-grounded tests for systematically evaluating AI coding agents.
r: EC6: tests agent robustness and behavioural anomalies (CLI, file operations), not code development at feature or project level.

q: Moreover, each phase is instantiated through a set of specialized agents designed to collaborate effectively across the pipeline.
r: EC6: new multi-agent framework limited to one specialised domain (ML paper reproduction), no contribution to the evaluation method.

q: This critical scoping review maps 348 studies and applies a five-step interpretation procedure to 94 comparison and diagnostic records from 42 studies, reading every inconsistent record against its source.
r: IC1: scoping review of component replacement in LLM agents in general, not about coding agents.

q: SWE-Bench++, an automated framework that generates repository-level coding tasks from open-source GitHub projects.
r: EC6: SWE-bench style benchmark built from pull requests (mostly bug fixes) and training trajectories, i.e. issue repair.

q: We introduce Code Primitives, agent-native reusable executable components that carry their own interface contracts, dependency closures, validation tests, and provenance.
r: EC5: main contribution is a new technique (reusable primitives, LEGO) compared on benchmarks, with little contribution to evaluation method.

q: We introduce Adaptive Skill Granularity, a framework that treats skill granularity as an action-abstraction policy conditioned on task structure, execution state, and macro-skill failures.
r: IC1: runtime skill-routing technique on a deterministic protocol, not context files or a study of coding agents on development tasks.

q: we introduce Website-derived Visual Skill Extraction (WebViSE), a framework that automatically abstracts these implementations into reusable Visual Skills and builds a structured Skill library.
r: IC1: visual design skill library for LLM website generation, not coding-agent context mechanisms or agent evaluation.
